items.title: PPI inflation report October 2026:
items.excerpt: Published Fri, Nov 13 2026 8:31 AM EST Updated 5 Hours Ago ... - The producer price index, a measure of wholesale prices, rose 0.3% in October, slightly less than the 0.4% forecast. - On an annual basis, PPI surged 6.5%, the biggest increase since November 2022. ... Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon. The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations. On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022. The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike. Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed. Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected. The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI. However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal. "Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management. Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched. "We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way." Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October. Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022. Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight. "We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks." Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

items.title: Bessent, Fed’s Goolsbee divided on role of energy shock in inflation By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Federal Reserve should not hike rates because of inflation driven by an "energy supply shock" tied to the Iran war, comments made to CNBC and promptly contradicted on the network by Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who said price pressures were building far beyond what could be explained by high oil prices. "I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock," while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC. "So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it’s coming down, these are very noisy numbers...You know, the Fed’s supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror." Shortly afterwards, the network hosted Goolsbee, a regular guest on CNBC’s morning Squawk Box show, who said that inflation was not just due to energy, but had spread to the service sector and areas like medical care that are not usually responsive to the price of oil, and was also elevated through strong demand tied to the AI data center buildout. "I respect the secretary and I am trying to figure out the same thing he is trying to figure out, which is how persistent is this inflation? The tariff inflation and oil price shock were supposed to have gone away by now and it hasn’t," Goolsbee said. "One puzzle is why have those supply shocks been as persistent as they have been. A second thing is if demand is overheating and that is contributing to inflation, that is more worrisome... Services inflation, which is probably not coming from tariffs or oil, is one of the more troubling aspects of the inflation reports we have been getting." While not committing to a rate hike, he said the Fed "has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility." ... But as inflation remained lodged above the Fed’s target, concern about it grew, as did ... Research meanwhile opened a different window on the relationship between oil prices and US inflation. Because the US is an energy exporter, higher global oil prices can filter through to the economy in the form of higher corporate profits and wages, providing a source of inflation beyond supply issues that can’t be easily ignored by the central bank.

items.title: Fed likely to need to raise rates amid worsening inflation: Daly By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 13 (Reuters) - San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Friday that her "bias" is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, particularly with services inflation moving in the wrong direction and some signs of inflation persistence. "We’re going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving," Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event. "Producers are telling us more and more that they’re running out of room to take it out of margins, and they really want to consider passing along this to consumers. So that’s the inflationary impulse we want to avoid." The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3% month over month in each of the last three months. That’s far higher than the 0.2% or less that would be consistent with year-over-year inflation at 2%, the Fed’s target. Daly, like several other policymakers, said she’s particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing is "not moving in the correct direction," which is particularly troubling because that slice of inflation tends to be sticky. "That’s a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, maybe they’re going to pass that along to customers," she said. The Fed raised its policy rate in September but held it steady in October, and financial markets are betting heavily on quarter-point interest-rate hikes at each of the Fed’s December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings. Daly said she feels markets understand how the Fed sets rates in response to economic conditions, without remarking specifically on the timing of coming rate hikes. Daly said she is also paying close attention to consumer spending, which accounts for most of the US economy, as the December meeting approaches. "Consumer spending remains just surprisingly resilient; you just haven’t seen a pullback, so I think that’s the piece of information that I’m really looking for in the next one to two to three months: what happens in that, especially around the holiday season, do we see consumers giving up or do we see them keeping going even if prices rise?" Daly said. "Sitting here in Las Vegas...we’re just starting to hear that the consumer may be running out of gas. And we’re hearing that now in other states, not just Nevada."

items.title: Live updates: Potential 2028 Democratic contenders discuss what’s next after midterm victories
items.excerpt: ## Van Hollen says he won't run for president in 2028 Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., told reporters this afternoon that he was "no longer pursuing" a 2028 presidential campaign and instead will focus on his effort to become Senate Democrats' next majority leader. “I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call with the American people,” Van Hollen said, later definitively adding, "I'm not running in 2028." Van Hollen, who officially announced his bid for majority leader yesterday, had previously told NBC News that he was still "kicking the tires" on a potential 2028 run. He said today that he spoke to Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and that the pair understand "this will be a competition" as Schumer tries to earn another stint of leading the caucus. "I think it's important to give Senate Democrats a choice," Van Hollen said. "That's what we just gave voters all over the country, a choice. They chose change, and I think that the Democratic Caucus needs to be open to new ideas." Van Hollen called himself the "underdog in this race," adding that the "majority leader has lots of powers of incumbency to try to, you know, make deals or agreements with people." "That's actually part of the problem with the process," he said. "But I can tell you that a lot of my colleagues want to see a whole different approach to governing in the United States Senate and in the Senate Democratic Caucus." Van Hollen, who said in an interview with MS NOW last night that "over 10" senators have privately backed him for the role, told reporters today that "I'm not going to put out a number," but that he had just heard from more senators who will support his bid. He specifically noted the endorsement of Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota, who wrote in a post on X today that Van Hollen is "the leader and fighter we need to bring about real change, so no American is left behind." Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, another newcomer to the Senate, also pledged his support to Van Hollen last night. "As you well know, the majority of the new members, fresh off the campaign trail, fresh off listening to their constituents, have said they will not support the current majority leader for re-election, and they are answering the call of the American people for change," Van Hollen said.

items.title: New Music Friday November 13: U2, Dolly Parton, Enrique Iglesias, Offset, Wiz Khalifa, Fall Out Boy and More | Entertainment Tonight
items.excerpt: Published: 8:17 AM PST, November 13, 2026 ## Check out some of ET's favorite new music of the week! Happy New Music Friday! The weekend is here, which means more streaming, new playlists and the best that music has to offer -- and ET has you covered for everything in between. U2 and Dolly Parton's new song and Dolly's final recording "Torn" is out now from U2's 16th studio album, Carnaval De Luz. The song was co-written by U2, Dolly and Johnny McDaid and is a tender country song detailing broken family ties that holds wider resonances. Dolly recorded the song in Nashville in June this year, making it her final recorded vocal performance prior to her passing in August. Ahead of the track's release, a country version titled 'Torn' (Kent Wells Version) premiered on country radio on November 12. The Country Music Association and ABC have announced more performers for The 60th Annual CMA Awards. Taylor Swift will be performing, marking her much-anticipated return 13 years since her last performance. Luke Combs, Vince Gill, Megan Moroney, Mumford & Sons, Chris Stapleton, Lainey Wilson and Stephen Wilson Jr. have also been added to the lineup. Brothers Osborne, Luke Bryan, Halestorm, HARDY and Marcus King will come together to celebrate Brooks & Dunn, this year's recipients of the CMA Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award. Country Music's Biggest Night will air live on November 18 on ABC and Disney+ and next day on Hulu. P!NK has announced her first ever Las Vegas residency at Sphere, becoming the first solo female artist to headline Sphere. Promoted by Live Nation, she will bring perform at Sphere beginning September 29. ... Rosalía made history at Latin GRAMMY Awards again as she won Album of the Year for her album, Lux, marking the third time she has taken home the honor and making her the first woman to win the award as a lead artist that many times. Janet Jackson made a surprise appearance presenting Daddy Yankee with the Person of the Year award. Daddy Yankee was also honored at the 2026 Latin Recording Academy Person of the Year Gala and recognized for his nearly three-decade career as a driving force behind the globalization of reggaeton and for his humanitarian efforts. ... Olivia Dean was announced as Apple Music's Artist of the Year, recognizing her undeniable leap to stardom. She is the first UK artist to receive this honor. Olivia shared, "I love making music. It's the best thing in the world. I think being Apple's Artist of the Year feels really amazing. To be recognized as an artist that's made an impact is really cool." Alex Warren has announced his Finding (More) Family On The Road 2027 World Tour with special guests Bebe Stockwell and Faouzia. Alex made the announcement in a video with Eric Stonestreet declaring he is adding 26 more shows. Promoted by Live Nation, the 26-city North American leg kicks off on April 5 at Paycom Center in Oklahoma City, making stops in New York, Tampa, Raleigh and more before wrapping up in Birmingham, AL on May 16. ... Fall Out Boy released a new song "ACES" which marks their first new original single in over three years. They also announced a new global headline tour, Twilight of the Punks, which will be the biggest tour of their career with 36 dates performing at stadiums and arenas across Europe, the UK and North America in 2027. Promoted by Live Nation, the tour kicks off May 17 at Prague's O2 Arena. To celebrate their tour announcement, Fall Out Boy gave a surprise pop up show at Koreatown in Los Angeles this week. Thousands of fans showed up for the eight-song set including the live debut of their new single "ACES."
